questions.enonce_markdown:
(a) Match the examples of Terms in set "A" to their corresponding types in set "B". Not all the types may be used.

| SET A: Terms | SET B: Types |
|---|---|
| 1. Blind and Sight | a. Abstract |
| 2. Rights and Duties | b. Singular |
| 3. The president of Cameroon. | c. Correlative. |
| 4. Happiness | d. Contrary. |
| | e. Privative |

(4x1 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
- **1. Blind and Sight - e. Privative.** "Blind" expresses the lack of a quality (sight) that a being of that kind should normally have.
- **2. Rights and Duties - c. Correlative.** Each term implies the other: there is no right without a corresponding duty.
- **3. The president of Cameroon - b. Singular.** It refers to one definite individual.
- **4. Happiness - a. Abstract.** It names a quality considered apart from the persons who have it.

**Answer: 1-e, 2-c, 3-b, 4-a.** Type d (Contrary) is not used.
themes: O Level Logic - definition and division

questions.enonce_markdown:
(b) (i) When is a Term said to be Undistributed?

(ii) Give the components of a Hypothetical Proposition. (2x2 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(i)** A term is **undistributed** when the proposition refers to only part of the class the term denotes, not to all its members. Example: in "Some students are lazy" the subject "students" is undistributed. (In the four standard forms: the subject of I and O and the predicate of A and I are undistributed.)

**(ii)** The components of a hypothetical proposition are the **antecedent** (the "if" clause), the **consequent** (the "then" clause) and the **implication**, the connective "if ... then" joining them.

questions.enonce_markdown:
(c) (i) Name two logicians who contributed to the development of Symbolic Logic.

(ii) Mention two importance of the use of symbols in Symbolic Logic. (2x2 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(i)** Any two of: **George Boole**, **Augustus De Morgan**, **Gottlob Frege**, **Gottfried Leibniz**, **Bertrand Russell** and **Alfred North Whitehead**.

**(ii)** Two importances of symbols:
- They remove the ambiguity and vagueness of ordinary language, so each symbol has one precise meaning.
- They show the form (structure) of an argument clearly and briefly, which makes it easy to test its validity (for example with truth tables), apart from the emotional effect of words.
themes: O Level Logic - symbolic logic basics

questions.enonce_markdown:
(d) (i) State the rule of Subcontrariety.

(ii) When is the Fallacy of Illicit Minor committed? (2x2 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(i)** Subcontraries are the I and O propositions with the same subject and predicate. **Rule:** they cannot both be false, but they can both be true. If one is false, the other is true; if one is true, the other is undetermined (doubtful).

**(ii)** The **fallacy of illicit minor** is committed when the minor term is distributed in the conclusion but is not distributed in the minor premise (a term may not be distributed in the conclusion unless it is distributed in its premise).

questions.enonce_markdown:
(e) (i) List two forms of a Mixed Hypothetical Syllogism.

(ii) Define an Informal Fallacy. (2x2 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(i)** The two valid forms of the mixed hypothetical syllogism are **Modus Ponens** (affirming the antecedent: If p then q; p; therefore q) and **Modus Tollens** (denying the consequent: If p then q; not q; therefore not p).

**(ii)** An **informal fallacy** is an error of reasoning that comes from the content, meaning or wording of the argument (irrelevant premises, ambiguity, unwarranted assumptions) and not from its logical form. It is found by examining what the argument says, not its pattern. Examples: appeal to force, equivocation.
